title: E-scooters on the pavement

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: The trial's being extended another year. Nine hundred scooters, and the complaints are almost entirely about parking rather than riding.

turns.speaker: Tobi
turns.text: Because a scooter left across a pavement is a wall if you can't see it.

turns.speaker: Meg
turns.text: That's the point the blind charities made and it took a long time for anyone to act on it.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: Docking bays fix most of it, and the cities that mandated them saw complaints fall sharply.

turns.speaker: Tobi
turns.text: At the cost of the thing that made them useful, which is leaving it where you finished.

turns.speaker: Meg
turns.text: Some cost is fine, though. Convenience for one person against passability for another isn't a close call.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: The injury data is the bit I find genuinely hard to read. Head injuries are high, helmet use is almost nil.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: Worse per mile, on most of the studies. Small wheels and a standing posture are unforgiving of a pothole.

turns.speaker: Meg
turns.text: Although a lot of those miles replaced a car journey, which has its own risk that nobody attributes to anyone.

turns.speaker: Tobi
turns.text: Did they replace car journeys, though? The surveys I've seen say mostly walking and buses.

turns.speaker: Lena
turns.text: That's right, and it's the finding that undercuts the environmental case almost completely.

turns.speaker: Meg
turns.text: So it's a convenience product with a climate story attached to it afterwards.

points: An e-scooter trial is extended, with complaints centring on parking rather than riding.
Scooters left across pavements obstruct blind and partially sighted people, a concern raised early by charities.
Mandatory docking bays sharply reduce complaints at the cost of convenience, which Meg considers an acceptable trade.
Injury data shows high head injuries with negligible helmet use, and worse rates per mile than cycling due to small wheels and standing posture.
Surveys indicate most journeys replaced walking and bus trips rather than car journeys.
Meg concludes the environmental case was attached afterwards to what is essentially a convenience product.
